laws.title: Constitution of 2020 — Presidential Power and State Structure
laws.subtitle: Algeria's revised constitution consolidating presidential authority
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's 2020 Constitution, approved by referendum with low turnout amid Hirak protest movement boycotts, reinforced the president's dominant role in the political system. The president appoints the prime minister, can dissolve parliament, and issues ordinances with legal force when parliament is in recess. Significant amendments included allowing Algerian military deployment abroad — a historic change — and provisions on Amazigh (Berber) language recognition as an official language alongside Arabic. Critics noted the constitution did not address fundamental demands of the Hirak movement for systemic democratic reform.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional framework; violations addressed through Constitutional Council review
exceptions: Amendments require two-thirds parliamentary approval or referendum
State of emergency provisions allow expanded presidential powers
National Security Council advises on defense and security matters

quiz.q: What historic military change did Algeria's 2020 Constitution introduce?
options: Creating a separate internal security force
Giving the military a parliamentary quota
quiz.explanation: Algeria's 2020 Constitution included a historically significant amendment allowing Algerian military forces to be deployed abroad for the first time.

laws.title: Penal Code — Political Offenses and Free Expression
laws.subtitle: Broad criminal provisions restricting dissent and political speech
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Penal Code contains numerous provisions that criminalize political dissent and speech. Article 96 criminalizes acts harming national unity; Articles 144–146 criminalize insult to the president, government institutions, and the military. The vague wording of these provisions has enabled prosecution of journalists, Hirak activists, and social media users. Amendments in 2021 introduced enhanced penalties for posting content deemed harmful to national security on social media. Algeria has one of the highest rates of journalist imprisonment in North Africa according to CPJ and RSF.
laws.penalty: 6 months–5 years imprisonment for political speech offenses; enhanced penalties for online speech
exceptions: Parliamentary immunity protects MPs for statements in legislative sessions
Academic publications with institutional backing may have more latitude
Foreign media operate under separate press accreditation rules

quiz.q: Which Algerian Penal Code articles criminalize insult to the president and institutions?
quiz.explanation: Articles 144–146 of Algeria's Penal Code criminalize insult to the president, government institutions, and the military, provisions widely used against dissidents.

laws.title: Military and Security Establishment — Constitutional Role
laws.subtitle: Algeria's powerful military and its relationship to civilian government
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's military (ANP — Armée Nationale Populaire) and intelligence services have historically been the dominant force in Algerian politics. The Department of Intelligence and Security (DRS, now DGSI after 2016 reforms) has pervasive influence. The military's constitutional role as guardian of the state gives it de facto veto power over civilian politics. The 1992 military coup that cancelled elections won by the Islamic Salvation Front led to a decade-long civil war. The 2019 ouster of President Bouteflika was orchestrated by military chief General Gaïd Salah. The military has resisted demands from the Hirak movement for a fully civilian transition.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional structure; civilian oversight of military formally exists but is limited in practice
exceptions: President is formally supreme commander of the armed forces
Parliament has nominal oversight of defense budget
Constitutional Council can review military-related legislation in theory

quiz.q: What major event demonstrated the Algerian military's political dominance in 2019?
options: Military coup overthrowing an elected government
Military chief orchestrating President Bouteflika's ouster
Military refusing to enforce civilian court orders
quiz.explanation: The 2019 ouster of long-serving President Bouteflika was orchestrated by military chief General Gaïd Salah, demonstrating the military's continued dominance in Algerian politics.

laws.title: Anti-Terrorism Law and Broad Security Provisions
laws.subtitle: Algeria's counter-terrorism framework with expansive definitions
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's anti-terrorism legislation, developed during and after the 1990s civil war, defines terrorism broadly to include acts disrupting state institutions or the national economy. The law grants extended pre-trial detention periods and allows prosecution before specialized terrorism chambers. Critics note the broad definition has been applied to political activists and Hirak participants. Algeria suffered devastating terrorist violence during the 1990s Black Decade — an estimated 100,000–200,000 deaths — which shaped the government's security-first approach. More recently the law has been applied against members of the Rachad movement and the MAK (Kabyle autonomy movement), both designated terrorist organizations.
laws.penalty: 10 years–life imprisonment for terrorism; death penalty for terrorism causing death
exceptions: Amnesty provisions exist for former combatants who surrendered under 1999/2006 reconciliation programs
Military courts have jurisdiction over some terrorism cases
Juveniles subject to separate procedures

quiz.q: Approximately how many people died in Algeria's 1990s civil war (Black Decade)?
quiz.explanation: An estimated 100,000–200,000 people died in Algeria's 1990s civil war (the Black Decade), following the military's cancellation of elections won by the Islamic Salvation Front.

laws.title: Hirak Movement and Assembly Law Restrictions
laws.subtitle: The 2019 popular uprising and legal crackdowns on assembly
laws.fullDescription: The Hirak Rif movement began in February 2019 as mass weekly protests against Bouteflika's fifth presidential term bid. After Bouteflika's removal, protests continued demanding systemic change. The government used the Penal Code, anti-terrorism provisions, and assembly restrictions to arrest hundreds of activists. Algeria's Law on Public Assemblies and Demonstrations requires prior authorization and has been used to ban protests. During COVID-19, gatherings were suspended. The Hirak resumed briefly in 2021 but further crackdowns intensified. UN human rights experts have called for release of political prisoners.
laws.penalty: Up to 1 year imprisonment for unauthorized assembly; anti-terrorism charges for organizers
exceptions: Trade union-authorized gatherings have different status
Religious gatherings in mosques treated differently
Authorized political party events require separate approval

quiz.q: When did Algeria's Hirak protest movement begin?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's Hirak protest movement began in February 2019 when mass weekly demonstrations erupted against President Bouteflika's bid for a fifth presidential term.

laws.title: Hydrocarbons Law — Oil and Gas Sector Regulation
laws.subtitle: Legal framework for Algeria's dominant oil and gas economy
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's economy is overwhelmingly dependent on hydrocarbons, which account for over 90% of export earnings and approximately 60% of government revenue. The state company Sonatrach is one of Africa's largest corporations. The Hydrocarbons Law has been revised multiple times — a 2019/2020 reform liberalized foreign investment rules to attract international partners after years of declining production. Unconventional gas (shale) development remains politically controversial; a 2015 fracking moratorium followed mass protests in southern Algeria. Algeria has significant natural gas reserves and is a major supplier to Europe.
laws.penalty: Heavy fines and contract cancellation for violations of hydrocarbons law; criminal referral for fraud
exceptions: Sonatrach's special status allows different operational rules than private companies
Exploration agreements govern specific contract areas
Emergency provisions allow accelerated development in strategic areas

quiz.q: What percentage of Algeria's export earnings come from hydrocarbons?
quiz.explanation: Hydrocarbons account for over 90% of Algeria's export earnings, making the economy almost entirely dependent on oil and gas production and prices.

laws.title: Religious Affairs Law — Non-Muslim Religious Practice
laws.subtitle: Restrictions on non-Islamic religious activity and proselytization
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Law No. 06-03 of 2006 regulates non-Muslim religious practice and strictly prohibits proselytization to Muslims. Non-Muslim religious gatherings must be held in approved premises, and all foreign religious materials must be authorized. Evangelical Christian communities — including Kabyle converts — have faced church closures, prosecutions, and deportation of foreign pastors under this law. Algeria's constitution declares Islam as the state religion. The National Commission on Non-Muslim Religions oversees implementation. International religious freedom organizations have documented systematic restrictions on Protestant Christian practice.
laws.penalty: 2–5 years imprisonment and fines for proselytizing to Muslims; fines for unauthorized religious gatherings
exceptions: Diplomatic community may practice non-Muslim religion in embassy premises
Recognized religious buildings predating the law may continue operating
Tourism-related religious services in hotels have different rules
laws.sourceLabel: US State Department Religious Freedom Report

quiz.q: What does Algeria's Law No. 06-03 of 2006 strictly prohibit?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's Law No. 06-03 strictly prohibits proselytization to Muslims, with penalties of 2–5 years imprisonment, and has been used to close churches and deport foreign pastors.

laws.title: Family Code of 1984 (Amended 2005) — Personal Status Law
laws.subtitle: Islamic family law governing marriage, divorce, and inheritance
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Family Code of 1984, influenced by Islamic jurisprudence, governs marriage, divorce, and inheritance for Muslim Algerians. Despite 2005 reforms improving women's rights, significant inequalities remain. Women cannot marry without a male guardian (wali), though reforms reduced this to a formality. Husbands can unilaterally divorce (talaq) while wives must seek judicial divorce on limited grounds. Inheritance follows Islamic rules giving daughters half a son's share. The minimum marriage age is 19 for both sexes. Polygamy (up to four wives) is permitted with judicial authorization. Non-Muslim Algerians are governed by civil law.
laws.penalty: N/A — civil family law; criminal consequences for violations of court orders
exceptions: Non-Muslim Algerians governed by civil personal status law
Algerians married abroad under foreign law have complex jurisdictional issues
Kabyle customary law (ith mquren) historically practiced but not formally recognized

quiz.q: What did Algeria's 2005 Family Code reforms change regarding female marriage requirements?
options: Eliminated the male guardian requirement entirely
Reduced the wali (male guardian) requirement to a formality
Required equal consent from both parties
quiz.explanation: Algeria's 2005 Family Code reforms reduced the wali (male guardian) requirement for women's marriage to a formality, though it was not eliminated entirely.

laws.title: Labour Law and Trade Union Rights
laws.subtitle: Algeria's labour framework and restrictions on independent unions
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's General Union of Algerian Workers (UGTA) was historically the sole legally recognized trade union under the single-party system. Since 1990, independent unions have been legally permitted but face registration obstacles and harassment. The Labour Law sets minimum wage (SNMG), working hours, and leave entitlements. Public sector workers dominate the unionized workforce. Strike rights exist legally but are restricted in essential services. Independent union leaders involved in Hirak-related protests have been arrested. The UGTA's close ties to the ruling FLN party compromise its independence.
laws.penalty: Fines for employers violating labour law; disciplinary action for workers participating in illegal strikes
exceptions: Essential services workers (healthcare, energy) face strike restrictions
Public sector employment governed by separate Civil Service Statute
Migrant agricultural workers face weaker enforcement of protections

quiz.q: What was historically the only legally recognized trade union in Algeria?
quiz.explanation: The General Union of Algerian Workers (UGTA) was historically Algeria's sole legally recognized trade union under the single-party system, though independent unions have been permitted since 1990.

laws.title: Cybercrime Law and Online Speech Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Algeria's prosecution of online dissent and social media content
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has dramatically increased prosecution of online speech since the Hirak movement. The Penal Code's Article 96 and anti-terrorism provisions have been applied to Facebook posts, YouTube videos, and WhatsApp messages. Journalists and activists have received prison terms of up to 10 years for online content. Algeria lacks a specific cybercrime law comparable to some neighbors but achieves the same result through Penal Code provisions applied to digital content. Internet penetration is approximately 70% and social media played a major role in coordinating Hirak protests. Authorities have blocked certain websites and VPN usage is common.
laws.penalty: 6 months–10 years imprisonment for online speech deemed harmful to state interests
exceptions: Strictly personal communications with no public distribution treated differently
Journalism accredited by Ministry of Communication has partial protection
Academic and research content may have some latitude

quiz.q: What legal provisions does Algeria primarily use to prosecute online speech?
options: Penal Code provisions applied to digital content
quiz.explanation: Algeria lacks a dedicated cybercrime law but uses existing Penal Code provisions — particularly Article 96 and anti-terrorism articles — applied to digital content to prosecute online speech.

laws.title: Banking and Finance Law — Algerian Currency Controls
laws.subtitle: Algeria's strict foreign exchange controls and banking regulation
laws.fullDescription: Algeria maintains strict foreign exchange controls under the Bank of Algeria Act and Finance Laws. The Algerian dinar is not convertible — Algerians cannot freely exchange dinars for foreign currency. Foreign currency accounts require special authorization. The parallel black market for foreign currency ('square port Said' in Algiers) persists despite crackdowns. Remittances from the large Algerian diaspora (particularly in France) are an important but under-tracked financial flow. Foreign investment repatriation of profits has historically faced restrictions, discouraging FDI. The 51/49 rule — requiring majority Algerian ownership of foreign investments — was partially relaxed in 2020 for non-strategic sectors.
laws.penalty: Fines and imprisonment for unauthorized foreign currency transactions; asset confiscation
exceptions: Tourism-related foreign currency transactions exempted from some controls
Diplomatic missions operate under separate currency rules
Import/export businesses authorized for foreign currency accounts

quiz.q: What was the controversial foreign investment rule that Algeria partially relaxed in 2020?
options: The 51/49 rule requiring majority Algerian ownership
quiz.explanation: Algeria's 51/49 rule required majority Algerian ownership in all foreign investments. It was partially relaxed in 2020 for non-strategic sectors to attract more foreign direct investment.

laws.title: Amazigh (Berber) Rights and Tamazight Language Recognition
laws.subtitle: Legal status of Algeria's Berber language and culture
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Berber (Amazigh) population, particularly concentrated in the Kabylie region, has historically fought for cultural and linguistic recognition. The 2002 constitution recognized Tamazight as a national language; the 2016 and 2020 constitutions elevated it to an official language alongside Arabic. The High Commission for Amazighness (HCA) promotes Tamazight. However, implementation has been slow — Arabic remains dominant in official functions and education. The MAK (Kabylie self-government movement), designated a terrorist organization in 2021, has pushed for Kabylie autonomy, leading to significant political crackdowns on Kabyle activists.
laws.penalty: N/A — language rights framework; MAK membership subject to anti-terrorism prosecution
exceptions: Tamazight-language education introduced but inconsistently implemented
Some municipalities in Kabylie use Tamazight in local administration
Cultural events in Tamazight permitted with appropriate authorization

quiz.q: When was Tamazight elevated to an official language in Algeria's constitution?
quiz.explanation: The 2016 constitution elevated Tamazight to an official language alongside Arabic. The 2002 constitution had only recognized it as a national language.

laws.title: Amnesty and National Reconciliation Law of 2006
laws.subtitle: Algeria's post-civil war reconciliation and amnesty framework
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation (Law No. 06-01 of 2006), approved by referendum, offered amnesty to former armed group members who surrendered and provided a framework to close the chapter on the 1990s civil war. Critically, Article 46 criminalizes any speech that 'tarnishes' the image of the state's institutions or security forces, effectively preventing discussion or accountability for atrocities committed by security forces during the Black Decade. Families of disappeared persons have been prosecuted for speaking publicly about their relatives' disappearances. The law has been condemned by human rights organizations for entrenching impunity.
laws.penalty: 3–5 years imprisonment for violating Article 46 by criticizing security forces' actions during the civil war
exceptions: Amnesty beneficiaries who reoffend lose protections
Foreign journalists face deportation rather than prosecution for violations
Academic research in certain forms has some latitude

quiz.q: What does Article 46 of Algeria's 2006 Reconciliation Law prohibit?
options: Speech that 'tarnishes' state institutions or security forces
quiz.explanation: Article 46 of Algeria's National Reconciliation Law criminalizes speech that 'tarnishes' the image of state institutions or security forces, preventing accountability for civil war atrocities.

laws.title: Audiovisual Law of 2014 — Media Licensing and State Control
laws.subtitle: Algeria's framework governing broadcast media
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Audiovisual Law of 2014 ended the legal monopoly of state television but in practice continued state dominance through the licensing authority (ARAV). Private television channels must obtain ARAV licenses, which have been denied or revoked for outlets critical of the government. Many Algerian private TV channels broadcast from abroad (primarily France) to avoid domestic licensing requirements. The state channels ENTV and Channel 3 dominate domestic broadcasting. Online media faces Penal Code-based restrictions. Algeria's press freedom ranking by RSF is consistently among the lowest in North Africa.
laws.penalty: Fines and forced closure for unauthorized broadcasting; criminal referral for content violations
exceptions: Foreign broadcasts received in Algeria cannot be blocked at source
Satellite television from abroad reaches wide audiences despite licensing restrictions
Online streaming platforms operate in grey area not covered by audiovisual law

quiz.q: Where do many Algerian private TV channels broadcast from to avoid domestic licensing?
quiz.explanation: Many Algerian private television channels broadcast from France to avoid Algeria's domestic licensing requirements enforced by the ARAV regulatory authority.

laws.title: Environmental Protection Law and Sahara Conservation
laws.subtitle: Algeria's environmental framework for its vast territory
laws.fullDescription: Algeria is Africa's largest country by area, with the Sahara Desert comprising over 80% of its territory. The Environment Law establishes the Ministry of Environment as the primary regulatory body. Algeria has significant biodiversity in its northern coastal regions and the Hoggar Mountains in the Sahara. The Ahaggar National Park is a major protected area. Oil and gas extraction in the Sahara raises environmental concerns — the In Salah gas field and proposed fracking projects face opposition from southern communities. Algeria participates in the UN Convention to Combat Desertification and has invested in the Great Green Wall initiative for the Sahel.
laws.penalty: Fines for environmental violations; facility shutdowns; criminal prosecution for egregious damage
exceptions: Hydrocarbons sector has historically received weaker environmental oversight
Military installation zones exempt from civilian environmental monitoring
Traditional pastoral routes recognized in Saharan protected areas

quiz.q: What percentage of Algeria's territory is covered by the Sahara Desert?
quiz.explanation: The Sahara Desert comprises over 80% of Algeria's territory, making it Africa's largest country by area but with most of its population concentrated in the northern coastal regions.

laws.title: Electoral Law and Single-Party Legacy
laws.subtitle: Algeria's electoral system and the FLN's political dominance
laws.fullDescription: Algeria transitioned from a formal one-party state (FLN — National Liberation Front) to multi-party elections in 1989 following mass riots. However, genuine political competition remains restricted. The Constitutional Council vets presidential candidates, with recent elections seeing most serious opposition candidates excluded. The 2019 presidential election was held amid Hirak protests and boycotts, with Tebboune winning with low turnout. Parliamentary elections similarly see low turnout amid widespread disillusionment. The FLN and its allied RND party maintain structural advantages including access to state resources.
laws.penalty: N/A — electoral framework; electoral fraud subject to criminal prosecution
exceptions: Independent candidates may run for parliamentary seats in theory
Opposition parties may field candidates but face registration obstacles
International election observers allowed but with limited access

quiz.q: What was Algeria's status before 1989 regarding political parties?
quiz.explanation: Algeria was a formal one-party state under the FLN (National Liberation Front) until 1989 when, following mass riots, the constitution was amended to allow multi-party competition.

laws.title: Death Penalty — Legal Status and Moratorium
laws.subtitle: Algeria's retained death penalty and de facto moratorium
laws.fullDescription: Algeria retains the death penalty in law for murder, terrorism, rape causing death, and treason, but has maintained a de facto moratorium on executions since 1993. During the civil war period, summary executions occurred outside formal legal processes. The last official judicial execution was in 1993. Algeria has not ratified the Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR aiming at abolition. Human rights organizations advocate for formal abolition. Death sentences continue to be handed down by courts — particularly for terrorism cases — but are commuted in practice. Algeria abstained on UN General Assembly resolutions calling for a global execution moratorium.
laws.penalty: Death penalty (not currently carried out); sentenced prisoners held on death row
exceptions: Minors cannot be sentenced to death
Pregnant women and mothers of young children protected from execution
Mental illness grounds for commutation

quiz.q: Since when has Algeria maintained a de facto moratorium on executions?
quiz.explanation: Algeria has maintained a de facto moratorium on executions since 1993, though the death penalty remains on the books and sentences continue to be handed down for terrorism and murder cases.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Law — Criminalization Under the Penal Code
laws.subtitle: Algeria's criminalization of same-sex relations
laws.fullDescription: Same-sex sexual relations are criminalized under Article 338 of Algeria's Penal Code with penalties of 2 months to 2 years imprisonment and fines. Social attitudes are overwhelmingly conservative, and LGBTQ+ people face significant societal discrimination. There are no legal protections for same-sex relationships and no recognition of same-sex partnerships. Online surveillance has reportedly been used to entrap gay men. Algerians who are openly LGBTQ+ typically do so only in private or after emigrating. Algeria's constitution does not address sexual orientation.
laws.penalty: 2 months–2 years imprisonment and fines for same-sex relations
exceptions: No formal exceptions — law applies to all same-sex activity
Enforcement more rigorous in rural than urban areas in practice
Foreign tourists may receive different treatment than citizens

quiz.q: What are the penalties under Article 338 of Algeria's Penal Code for same-sex relations?
quiz.explanation: Article 338 of Algeria's Penal Code criminalizes same-sex sexual relations with penalties of 2 months to 2 years imprisonment and fines.

laws.title: Land Law and Post-Independence Property Nationalization
laws.subtitle: Algeria's complex land tenure system following colonial-era expropriation
laws.fullDescription: Algeria nationalized vast amounts of agricultural land following independence from France in 1962, expropriating colonial settlers' (pieds-noirs) land. The 1971 Agrarian Revolution further redistributed land to cooperatives. Economic liberalization from the 1990s privatized some state-held land but significant public ownership remains. Urban land tenure is complex, with widespread informal housing ('bidonvilles') particularly around Algiers. Squatter settlements are periodically demolished and residents relocated, sometimes forcibly. Foreign ownership of agricultural land is prohibited. The state retains significant commercial and industrial property.
laws.penalty: N/A — state land authority; unauthorized construction faces demolition orders
exceptions: Former colonial property claims from pieds-noirs are not recognized by Algerian courts
Waqf (religious endowment) properties follow separate Islamic law
Special economic zones have different land tenure arrangements

quiz.q: When did Algeria nationalize colonial settlers' agricultural land?
quiz.explanation: Algeria nationalized vast agricultural land from colonial settlers (pieds-noirs) following independence from France in 1962, with further redistribution through the 1971 Agrarian Revolution.

laws.title: Import/Export Regulations and Protectionist Trade Policy
laws.subtitle: Algeria's restrictive trade regime protecting domestic industry
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has historically maintained protectionist trade policies to develop domestic industry and reduce import dependency. Temporary import bans on hundreds of products were imposed from 2018–2020 to conserve foreign exchange. Local content requirements favor domestically produced goods. Algeria's trade relationship with the EU is governed by the 2002 Association Agreement, though Algeria has been slow to implement full trade liberalization. Algeria is not a WTO member (though in accession negotiations). The customs code was revised in 2017 to tighten import controls and increase enforcement against smuggling across the vast Saharan borders.
laws.penalty: Heavy customs fines; confiscation of goods; imprisonment for smuggling
exceptions: Diplomatic goods exempt from customs duties
Humanitarian aid imports under specific exemption frameworks
Free zone operations in Bellara and other industrial zones

quiz.q: What significant trade restriction did Algeria implement from 2018–2020?
options: Temporary import bans on hundreds of products to conserve foreign exchange
Withdrawal from the EU Association Agreement
quiz.explanation: Algeria imposed temporary import bans on hundreds of product categories from 2018–2020 to conserve foreign exchange reserves as oil prices fell.

laws.title: Intelligence Services — DRS/DGSI Powers
laws.subtitle: Algeria's feared intelligence apparatus and its legal framework
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's intelligence service, restructured from the DRS (Department of Intelligence and Security) to the DGSI (General Directorate of Internal Security) in 2016, has historically operated with near-total autonomy. The DRS under General Mohamed Mediene (Toufik) was considered the de facto ruler of Algeria for much of the 1990s–2010s. The intelligence services have broad surveillance and detention powers with minimal judicial oversight. Hirak activists, Islamists, and journalists have been monitored and prosecuted using intelligence-gathered evidence. The restructuring was partly an attempt by President Bouteflika to reassert civilian control before his 2019 ouster.
laws.penalty: N/A — operates largely outside normal criminal law; formal charges required eventually
exceptions: Constitutional provisions nominally limit arbitrary detention
International human rights bodies may visit facilities in limited circumstances
Formal criminal charges must accompany prolonged detention in theory

quiz.q: What was Algeria's intelligence service restructured from DRS to in 2016?
quiz.explanation: Algeria restructured its intelligence service from the DRS (Department of Intelligence and Security) to the DGSI (General Directorate of Internal Security) in 2016, partly as an attempt at civilian reassertion of control.

laws.title: Sub-Saharan African Migration — Crackdowns and Deportations
laws.subtitle: Algeria's treatment of sub-Saharan African migrants and asylum seekers
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has become a major transit country for sub-Saharan African migrants attempting to reach Europe via the Mediterranean. Algeria has conducted large-scale roundups and deportations of migrants, including asylum seekers, to the Niger and Mali borders — in some cases abandoning people in the desert without water. Human Rights Watch and other organizations have documented these summary deportations as violating international law. Algeria has not ratified the 1951 Refugee Convention. The IOM estimates tens of thousands of migrants are expelled annually. Sub-Saharan African migrants face discrimination and racial violence in Algerian society.
laws.penalty: Administrative detention and forced deportation for irregular migrants; criminal charges for smuggling networks
exceptions: UNHCR-registered asylum seekers theoretically entitled to protection in practice often deported anyway
Students with valid visas not subject to migration enforcement
Diplomatic negotiations occasionally pause deportations

quiz.q: What international document has Algeria NOT ratified that would protect asylum seekers?
quiz.explanation: Algeria has not ratified the 1951 Refugee Convention, giving it no formal legal obligations to asylum seekers, and has conducted mass deportations to desert border areas.

laws.title: State of Emergency History and Current Security Powers
laws.subtitle: Algeria's emergency law record and residual security legislation
laws.fullDescription: Algeria maintained a state of emergency from 1992 to 2011 — nearly 20 years — following the military's cancellation of elections won by the Islamist FIS party. The emergency was used to justify mass detentions, restrictions on assembly, and security force impunity. It was lifted nominally in 2011 in response to Arab Spring pressure, but many emergency-era powers were preserved in ordinary legislation including the anti-terrorism law and national reconciliation law. COVID-19 pandemic restrictions in 2020 were implemented under health law. Algeria's experience demonstrates how emergency powers once normalized can become permanent features of governance.
laws.penalty: Historical; residual powers maintained through ordinary legislation post-2011
exceptions: Constitution retains presidential power to declare state of emergency with parliamentary approval
Regional or local states of emergency can be declared for natural disasters
International human rights monitoring nominally permitted

quiz.q: How long did Algeria's state of emergency last from its declaration in 1992?
quiz.explanation: Algeria maintained a state of emergency from 1992 to 2011 — nearly 20 years — using it to justify mass detentions and security force impunity following the military's cancellation of Islamist electoral victory.

laws.title: National Health System and Pharmaceutical Policy
laws.subtitle: Algeria's public healthcare system and medicines regulation
laws.fullDescription: Algeria operates a largely public healthcare system funded by hydrocarbon revenues, providing nominally free healthcare to citizens. The quality of public healthcare has declined following fiscal constraints from falling oil prices. Private healthcare has expanded significantly. Algeria has a domestic pharmaceutical industry and policies promoting generic drug production and import substitution. The National Agency for Pharmaceutical Products (ANPP) regulates medicines. Brain drain of medical professionals emigrating to France is a significant challenge. Algeria's healthcare indicators — infant mortality, life expectancy — are moderate by regional standards.
laws.penalty: N/A — regulatory system; pharmaceutical fraud subject to criminal prosecution
exceptions: Emergency treatment must be provided regardless of insurance status
Medicines on the essential medicines list are heavily subsidized
Private clinics subject to quality inspections by health ministry

options: Brain drain of doctors emigrating to France
Exclusion of women from medical careers
quiz.explanation: Brain drain of medical professionals emigrating to France is a significant challenge for Algeria's healthcare system, contributing to quality decline in public facilities.

laws.title: Anti-Corruption Laws and Bouteflika-Era Prosecutions
laws.subtitle: Algeria's anti-corruption framework and high-profile prosecutions
laws.fullDescription: Following President Bouteflika's removal in 2019, Algeria launched unprecedented corruption prosecutions against former senior officials including former prime ministers, intelligence chiefs, and tycoons from the Bouteflika era. These trials were widely seen as politically motivated selective accountability rather than systematic anti-corruption reform. The 2006 Law on Prevention and Fight Against Corruption established the formal framework but was poorly enforced during the Bouteflika years. The National Office for Prevention and Fight Against Corruption (ONPLCC) coordinates enforcement. Transparency International ranks Algeria poorly on its Corruption Perceptions Index.
laws.penalty: 5–10 years imprisonment for corruption; enhanced penalties for officials; asset forfeiture
exceptions: Military corruption handled through military justice system
Cases involving state secrets may be tried in closed proceedings
Cooperation with prosecutors can reduce sentences

quiz.q: What event triggered Algeria's unprecedented corruption prosecutions of former officials?
quiz.explanation: Following President Bouteflika's removal in 2019, Algeria launched unprecedented corruption prosecutions against former prime ministers, intelligence chiefs, and oligarchs from the Bouteflika era.

laws.title: Water Law and Management of Scarce Water Resources
laws.subtitle: Algeria's water policy framework and desalination investments
laws.fullDescription: Algeria faces significant water stress despite being larger than Western Europe. The National Agency for Water Resources manages surface and groundwater. Algeria has invested heavily in seawater desalination — the Hamma plant near Algiers is one of Africa's largest. The Albien aquifer (shared with Libya and Tunisia) is an important fossil groundwater source. Rapid urbanization and agriculture account for 65% of water use. Water pricing below cost recovery encourages waste. Climate change is projected to reduce rainfall in northern Algeria by 20–30% by 2050. Industrial water pollution, particularly near Oran, is a significant concern.
laws.penalty: Fines for unauthorized water extraction; pollution discharge violations subject to administrative and criminal penalties
exceptions: Agricultural water use historically subsidized
Emergency drought provisions allow temporary water restrictions
Humanitarian exemptions for refugee and displacement camp water supply
laws.sourceLabel: National Agency for Water Resources Algeria

quiz.q: What percentage of Algeria's water use goes to agriculture?
quiz.explanation: Agriculture accounts for approximately 65% of Algeria's water use, with water pricing below cost recovery levels encouraging waste in a water-stressed country.

laws.title: Education Law and Arabization Policy
laws.subtitle: Algeria's Arabic-language education policy and its impact
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Arabization policy, implemented progressively from independence, made Arabic the exclusive language of instruction in public schools, replacing French and Tamazight. The policy, pursued through the 1990s, is now seen by many economists as having harmed Algeria's competitive position since French remains dominant in business, higher education, and technical fields. The education system has struggled with quality — significant percentages of students cannot read proficiently by age 10. University enrollment is high but graduate unemployment is widespread. The curriculum includes Islamic education as a mandatory subject. Education policy has been politically contentious, with debates over the role of French, Tamazight, and English.
laws.penalty: N/A — educational framework
exceptions: Private French-language schools exist and are popular with elites
University programs in medicine and sciences use some French and English
Tamazight education introduced gradually in Kabyle-majority areas

quiz.q: What language did Algeria's Arabization policy replace as the language of instruction?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's Arabization policy progressively replaced French (the colonial language) with Arabic as the exclusive language of instruction in public schools, a policy now criticized for reducing economic competitiveness.

laws.title: Forced Disappearances — Civil War Legacy
laws.subtitle: Unresolved disappearances from the 1990s civil war
laws.fullDescription: Between 7,000–18,000 people disappeared during Algeria's 1990s civil war — taken by security forces or armed groups. The National Reconciliation Law of 2006 effectively closed accountability for these disappearances and criminalized families who publicly demanded information. The state paid compensation to some families conditioned on accepting that their relative is dead and abandoning legal claims. International human rights mechanisms including the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances have criticized Algeria's refusal to investigate and prosecute perpetrators. Algeria refuses to allow international investigations, citing sovereignty.
laws.penalty: 3–5 years imprisonment under Article 46 of the Reconciliation Law for family members who publicly discuss disappearances
exceptions: Private discussions between families and lawyers technically not criminalized
International human rights bodies can receive complaints but have no enforcement mechanism
Some cases reopened where perpetrators made public confessions

quiz.q: How many people are estimated to have disappeared during Algeria's 1990s civil war?
quiz.explanation: Between 7,000–18,000 people disappeared during Algeria's 1990s civil war, taken by security forces or armed groups, with the 2006 Reconciliation Law effectively closing accountability for these cases.

laws.title: EU Association Agreement and Trade Liberalization
laws.subtitle: Algeria's trade relationship with the European Union
laws.fullDescription: Algeria signed an Association Agreement with the EU in 2002 that entered into force in 2005, committing to progressive trade liberalization over 12 years. However, Algeria has been among the slowest Arab Mediterranean countries to implement the agreement, using safeguard clauses and import restrictions. In 2020, Algeria suspended annual review meetings with the EU over political disagreements. The EU is Algeria's largest trade partner — mainly for hydrocarbon exports — but the relationship is complicated by migration pressures, Hirak-era human rights concerns, and competition from China. Algeria has considered renegotiating the agreement.
laws.penalty: N/A — trade framework; WTO-type dispute mechanisms apply
exceptions: Sensitive agricultural goods subject to longer liberalization timelines
Anti-dumping measures permitted for domestic industries under serious threat
Strategic industries explicitly carved out from liberalization

quiz.q: When did Algeria's Association Agreement with the EU enter into force?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's Association Agreement with the EU was signed in 2002 and entered into force in 2005, committing to progressive trade liberalization though Algeria has been slow to implement its terms.

laws.title: Housing Law and Social Housing Programs
laws.subtitle: Algeria's public housing construction and distribution system
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has one of the world's most ambitious public housing programs — over a million social housing units (AADL, LSP, LPA) built since 2000 using hydrocarbon revenues. The system involves state-subsidized construction by public enterprise AADL with allocation through lottery systems. Despite massive construction, housing demand from population growth continues to exceed supply. Quality of construction has been criticized, with some developments having structural problems. Corruption in housing allocation — selling lottery spots or obtaining units through connections — is a persistent problem. Slum clearance programs have sometimes displaced residents without adequate replacement housing.
laws.penalty: N/A — housing entitlement system; fraud against housing programs prosecuted
exceptions: Priority allocation for earthquake victims and natural disaster displaced persons
Special programs for military and security personnel
Rural housing programs have different criteria than urban programs

quiz.q: What is Algeria's primary vehicle for mass public housing construction?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's AADL (Agence Nationale de l'Amélioration et du Développement du Logement) program is the primary vehicle for mass state-subsidized housing construction, part of one of the world's most ambitious public housing programs.

laws.title: Western Sahara Policy — Algeria's Support for Polisario Front
laws.subtitle: Algeria's role in the Western Sahara conflict
laws.fullDescription: Algeria hosts the Polisario Front, the independence movement of Western Sahara, and the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR) government-in-exile at Tindouf in southwestern Algeria. An estimated 100,000–170,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps near Tindouf. Algeria views Western Sahara's self-determination as a decolonization issue and provides diplomatic, logistical, and financial support to the Polisario. This is a major source of tension with Morocco, with the two countries having no diplomatic relations since 1994 and a closed border since 1994. The conflict has frozen Maghreb regional integration.
laws.penalty: N/A — foreign policy position
exceptions: Humanitarian aid organizations operate in Tindouf camps under separate arrangements
Polisario Front not treated as a terrorist organization in Algeria
UN negotiations on Western Sahara continue independently of Algeria's bilateral dispute with Morocco

quiz.q: Where does Algeria host the Polisario Front and Sahrawi refugee camps?
quiz.explanation: Algeria hosts the Polisario Front and Sahrawi refugee camps at Tindouf in southwestern Algeria, providing support to Western Saharan independence movement.

laws.title: Civil Service Statute and Public Sector Employment
laws.subtitle: Algeria's large public sector employment framework
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's public sector employs approximately 2.5 million people — one of the largest state payrolls in Africa relative to population. The General Civil Service Statute governs recruitment, promotion, discipline, and dismissal of civil servants. Public employment has historically served as a social contract absorbing university graduates in the absence of sufficient private sector jobs. Fiscal constraints from falling oil prices have forced some rationalization, but significant overstaffing persists in state enterprises. Civil servants have job security protections that make dismissal difficult except for disciplinary cause.
laws.penalty: Dismissal procedures for misconduct; criminal prosecution for abuse of public function
exceptions: Probationary period before permanent civil service status
Senior officials (walis, directors-general) appointed and dismissed by president
Military civil servants governed by separate statute

quiz.q: Approximately how many people does Algeria's public sector employ?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's public sector employs approximately 2.5 million people, one of the largest state payrolls in Africa relative to population, reflecting hydrocarbon-funded public employment policies.

laws.title: Customs Law and Informal Economy
laws.subtitle: Regulation of Algeria's vast informal trading sector
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's informal economy is estimated at 30–40% of GDP. The customs code was tightened in 2017 to reduce the square (informal currency exchange and goods trading). Traditional informal markets called 'trabendo' have historically provided employment and affordable goods outside formal channels. The government has periodically cracked down — demolishing informal market areas — then tolerated the activity due to its social role. Smuggling across Algeria's vast desert borders with Mali, Niger, and Libya is significant. The authorities struggle to enforce formal trade rules given the sheer size of Algeria's territory.
laws.penalty: Fines and confiscation for customs violations; imprisonment for organized smuggling networks
exceptions: Small-scale cross-border trading by border communities treated more leniently
Agricultural produce from neighboring countries historically tolerated
Amnesty periods for customs regularization have been offered periodically

quiz.q: What percentage of Algeria's GDP is estimated to come from the informal economy?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's informal economy is estimated at 30–40% of GDP, with traditional informal markets called 'trabendo' historically providing employment and affordable goods outside formal channels.

laws.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Response and Health Emergency Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's legal framework for pandemic management
laws.fullDescription: Algeria managed the COVID-19 pandemic response primarily through executive orders and health ministry regulations rather than dedicated pandemic legislation. Curfews, public gathering restrictions, and business closures were implemented under the Defence Law. Algeria was relatively slow to procure vaccines — the AstraZeneca vaccine was rolled out from early 2021. A vaccine skepticism culture, partly linked to Islamic views on vaccine ingredients, complicated the rollout. Algeria developed domestic vaccine production ambitions. The pandemic also revealed significant weaknesses in hospital capacity and oxygen supply chains.
laws.penalty: Fines for violation of pandemic health orders; business closures for non-compliant establishments
exceptions: Essential services exempted from closure orders
Religious gatherings subject to capacity limits rather than full prohibition initially
International medical NGOs operating under special authorizations

quiz.q: Under what law did Algeria implement COVID-19 curfews and restrictions?
quiz.explanation: Algeria implemented COVID-19 pandemic restrictions including curfews under the Defence Law rather than dedicated pandemic legislation, enabling executive action without parliamentary approval.

laws.title: Forest Fire Law and Climate Change Vulnerability
laws.subtitle: Algeria's response to devastating wildfires
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has experienced devastating wildfires, particularly in the Kabylie region. The August 2021 fires killed over 90 people and destroyed tens of thousands of hectares of forest. Arson — including politically motivated fires — has been alleged, and several people were arrested in connection with fire-setting, with some facing the death penalty under a 2020 law that introduced capital punishment for arson causing deaths. Algeria's forest cover is already minimal — approximately 1% of territory. Climate change is increasing fire risk. The Forest Administration manages fire prevention and response.
laws.penalty: Death penalty for arson causing deaths (introduced 2020); heavy imprisonment for other arson
exceptions: Accidental fires treated differently from deliberate arson
Traditional agricultural burning with permits treated separately
Civil liability for fire damage separate from criminal prosecution

quiz.q: What new penalty did Algeria introduce in 2020 for arson causing deaths?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's 2020 law introduced the death penalty for arson causing deaths, implemented following devastating wildfires that killed over 90 people in the Kabylie region in 2021.

laws.title: Women's Rights — Legal Status and Practical Barriers
laws.subtitle: Algerian women's legal position and social constraints
laws.fullDescription: Algerian women have formal legal equality in constitutional terms, but the Family Code creates significant inequalities in personal status. Women's labor force participation is approximately 18% — low by international standards. Violence against women is criminalized — the 2015 amendment to the Penal Code introduced specific provisions against domestic violence with penalties of 6 months–20 years imprisonment. However, enforcement is inconsistent and social pressure often discourages reporting. Femicide statistics are concerning. Women have made gains in education — girls now outnumber boys in universities — and in some professional fields.
laws.penalty: 6 months–20 years imprisonment for domestic violence under 2015 Penal Code amendments
exceptions: Family reconciliation is legally permitted and culturally encouraged even in domestic violence cases
Marital rape not explicitly criminalized under current law
Traditional practices in rural areas may receive different treatment

quiz.q: When did Algeria introduce specific Penal Code provisions against domestic violence?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's 2015 amendment to the Penal Code introduced specific provisions against domestic violence, prescribing penalties of 6 months to 20 years imprisonment.

laws.title: Blasphemy and Contempt of Islam Law
laws.subtitle: Criminal penalties for insulting Islam or the Prophet
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Penal Code criminalizes blasphemy and insults to Islam, with penalties including imprisonment. Article 144 bis 2, added in 1994 during the civil war period, specifically prohibits insulting the Prophet Muhammad and may carry up to 5 years imprisonment. These provisions reflect the state's constitutional commitment to Islam as the state religion. Prosecutions have included Christians sharing religious materials, journalists, and social media users. The law has been applied to Kabyle activists accused of Ahmadi Muslim affiliation. Non-Muslims face particular vulnerability to these charges.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment and fines for blasphemy; enhanced penalties for public blasphemy through media
exceptions: Academic theological study within approved Islamic frameworks may be protected
Private expression between individuals less likely to be prosecuted
Foreign nationals typically deported rather than imprisoned
laws.sourceLabel: US State Department Religious Freedom Report

quiz.q: When was Algeria's specific prohibition against insulting the Prophet added to the Penal Code?
quiz.explanation: Article 144 bis 2, prohibiting insult to the Prophet Muhammad with up to 5 years imprisonment, was added to Algeria's Penal Code in 1994 during the civil war period.

laws.title: Public Works and Infrastructure Procurement
laws.subtitle: Algeria's massive infrastructure investment programs
laws.fullDescription: Algeria invested heavily in infrastructure using oil revenues during the 2000s commodity boom — roads, highways, railways, hospitals, and the Algiers metro. The East-West Highway connecting the Tunisian and Moroccan borders was one of the largest infrastructure projects in North Africa. Chinese and European companies won major contracts. The procurement framework for public works has been criticized for corruption and cost overruns — the East-West Highway budget expanded from $6 billion to over $11 billion. Following oil price declines, infrastructure spending was cut significantly. The 2019 corruption prosecutions targeted several businessmen involved in infrastructure contracts.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for procurement fraud; fines and disqualification from public contracts
exceptions: Emergency infrastructure procurement under natural disaster provisions
Defense infrastructure subject to classified procurement procedures
Foreign company participation governed by bilateral investment agreements

quiz.q: What was the final cost of Algeria's East-West Highway, far exceeding its original budget?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's East-West Highway budget expanded from an original $6 billion to over $11 billion, becoming a symbol of corruption and cost overruns in major infrastructure projects.

laws.title: Banned Organizations — FIS and Islamist Groups
laws.subtitle: Legal prohibition of the Islamic Salvation Front and related groups
laws.fullDescription: The Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), which won the first round of the 1991 legislative elections with an absolute majority, was dissolved by court order in 1992 after the military cancelled the elections. FIS membership or support is criminalized. Its armed wing, the AIS, reached a ceasefire with the government in 1997. Other Islamist groups designated as terrorist organizations include the GIA, GSPC (now AQIM — Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb), and JNIM. Algeria has been at the forefront of regional counter-terrorism cooperation in the Sahel region.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution and imprisonment for membership in banned organizations; terrorism charges for armed group participation
exceptions: Amnesty provisions of 2006 applied to former armed group members who surrendered
Non-violent former FIS members may not face prosecution
AIS fighters who accepted the ceasefire received amnesty

quiz.q: Why was Algeria's FIS (Islamic Salvation Front) dissolved in 1992?
options: The military cancelled elections it had won and the party was dissolved by court order
It was found to have foreign funding
It failed to reach the electoral threshold
quiz.explanation: The FIS was dissolved by court order in 1992 after the military cancelled legislative elections the FIS had won in the first round, triggering Algeria's decade-long civil war.

laws.title: State Enterprise Privatization Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's framework for state-owned enterprise management
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has over 1,000 state-owned enterprises (EPEs — Entreprises Publiques Économiques) across sectors from steel to food processing. Unlike many economies, Algeria has resisted significant privatization — a major privatization program launched in the 1990s was largely abandoned. The Participation and Promotion of Investment Law regulates state enterprise governance. Strategic sectors including hydrocarbons, defense, and banking remain fully state-owned. Sonatrach (oil), Sonelgaz (energy), and Air Algérie are the flagship state enterprises. Management quality has been criticized and productivity lags private sector benchmarks.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for mismanagement and fraud in state enterprises; civil liability for losses
exceptions: Strategic sectors not subject to privatization requirements
International partners may hold minority stakes in otherwise state-controlled enterprises
Small state enterprises below a certain threshold sold to employees in some programs

quiz.q: How many state-owned enterprises does Algeria approximately have?
quiz.explanation: Algeria has over 1,000 state-owned enterprises (EPEs) across multiple sectors, reflecting the country's historically state-dominated economy that has resisted significant privatization.

laws.title: Conscription and Military Service Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's mandatory military service requirements
laws.fullDescription: Algeria maintains mandatory military service for male citizens aged 19–30. The basic service period is 12 months, including civic training. Algeria has a large active military of approximately 130,000 troops and significant reserve force. Military service is considered both a national security requirement and a social institution. Exemptions exist for sole breadwinners, students (deferment), and the medically unfit. Conscientious objection is not legally recognized. The military budget consumes approximately 6% of GDP — high by regional standards — sustained by hydrocarbon revenues.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution and imprisonment for draft evasion; disciplinary penalties within military
exceptions: University students may defer until completion of studies
Sole surviving sons of widows may be exempt
Medical unfitness is a recognized exemption

quiz.q: What is Algeria's mandatory military service period?
quiz.explanation: Algeria requires 12 months of mandatory military service for male citizens aged 19–30, with exemptions for students (who may defer), sole breadwinners, and the medically unfit.

laws.title: Political Party Restrictions — FLN Dominance
laws.subtitle: The National Liberation Front's structural political advantages
laws.fullDescription: The FLN (National Liberation Front) governed Algeria as a single party from independence until 1989. Since multiparty elections resumed, the FLN and its ally the RND have maintained dominance through access to state resources, media, and administrative machinery. Islamist parties must comply with the Associations Law provision banning parties based 'entirely on religion' — a constraint that has been applied selectively. The FLN's legitimacy is rooted in its role in the independence war. Since Bouteflika's FLN was linked to corruption, the party's public standing has fallen, though it retains structural advantages.
laws.penalty: Dissolution for parties violating registration requirements; criminal charges for parties receiving foreign funding
exceptions: Religious parties permitted if not 'exclusively' religious in character
Berber parties permitted but monitored for separatist tendencies
Military and security personnel prohibited from party membership

quiz.q: From when until when did the FLN govern Algeria as a single party?
quiz.explanation: The FLN governed Algeria as a single party from independence in 1962 until 1989, when following mass riots the constitution was amended to allow multiparty competition.

laws.title: Diaspora Engagement and Dual Nationality Policy
laws.subtitle: Algeria's relationship with its large diaspora in France
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has one of the world's largest diasporas — an estimated 3–5 million Algerians live in France, with significant communities also in Canada, Spain, and Gulf countries. Algeria permits dual nationality though this has been contested. The Algerian diaspora sends significant remittances. Second and third generation Algerians in France ('Beurs') have complex legal relationships with Algeria. The government has periodically tried to engage diaspora capital for investment while being suspicious of diaspora political activism — particularly those supportive of the Hirak or human rights criticism. Some diaspora activists have been detained upon return to Algeria.
laws.penalty: Potential legal issues if diaspora political activity deemed hostile to Algeria
exceptions: Dual nationality with France not formally recognized in all official contexts
Diaspora investment programs offer specific incentives
Children born abroad to Algerian parents acquire citizenship automatically
laws.sourceLabel: Algerian Ministry of National Community Abroad

quiz.q: Approximately how many Algerians live in France?
quiz.explanation: An estimated 3–5 million Algerians live in France, making the Algerian diaspora in France one of the world's largest diasporas relative to origin country population.

laws.title: Road Safety Law and Traffic Enforcement
laws.subtitle: Algeria's traffic regulations and road safety challenges
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has one of the highest road fatality rates in Africa and the world — approximately 3,000–4,000 people die annually on Algerian roads. The Traffic Code was revised in 2009 introducing a points system for licences. Alcohol is legally banned while driving (0.0% BAC). Enforcement is uneven, particularly outside urban areas. The national highway network has expanded significantly through public investment. Driver licensing standards have been criticized as inadequate. Road safety campaigns run by the National Security Road Committee have had limited impact.
laws.penalty: Fines and licence suspension for traffic violations; imprisonment for causing death through dangerous driving
exceptions: Military and emergency vehicles have operational exemptions
Agricultural vehicles in rural areas treated with less strictness
Diplomatic immunity applies to accredited diplomats

quiz.q: Approximately how many people die annually on Algeria's roads?
quiz.explanation: Algeria has approximately 3,000–4,000 annual road fatalities, one of the highest rates in Africa and the world, driven by poor enforcement, infrastructure, and driving standards.

laws.title: Foreign Exchange and Capital Controls
laws.subtitle: Algeria's restrictions on foreign currency and capital movement
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's foreign exchange system maintains strict controls under Bank of Algeria regulations. The official exchange rate and black market rate have diverged significantly in periods of oil price decline. Exporting foreign currency exceeding authorized limits is illegal. Foreign companies can repatriate profits but must comply with registration and reporting requirements. The parallel market for currency has persisted despite periodic crackdowns. Algeria's foreign exchange reserves peaked at $194 billion in 2014 before declining sharply. The 2020 collapse in oil prices created fiscal pressure leading to some relaxation of capital controls for import purposes.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment and fines for unauthorized foreign currency transactions; asset confiscation
exceptions: International travel allowances permit limited foreign currency purchases
Import businesses authorized for foreign currency through banking system
Diplomatic accounts exempt from controls

quiz.q: When did Algeria's foreign exchange reserves peak?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's foreign exchange reserves peaked at approximately $194 billion in 2014 before declining sharply as oil prices fell, creating fiscal pressure and prompting some relaxation of capital controls.

laws.title: Telecommunications Law and Internet Governance
laws.subtitle: Algeria's telecom regulatory framework and internet control
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's telecommunications sector was dominated by the state operator Algérie Télécom (for fixed lines and ADSL) and the mobile subsidiary Mobilis. Three mobile operators serve the market. The Electronic Communications Regulatory Authority (ARPT) oversees licensing and competition. Internet penetration is approximately 70%. The government has demonstrated willingness to throttle internet speeds during exams (to prevent cheating) and political events. Social media platforms WhatsApp and Facebook were restricted during 2019 Hirak protests. VPN usage is common to circumvent restrictions. Algeria has been slow to deploy 4G (launched 2016) and 5G.
laws.penalty: Fines for telecommunications violations; criminal prosecution for unauthorized interception of communications
exceptions: Government internet services operate on separate networks
Educational institutions may access additional bandwidth
Emergency communications services have priority access

quiz.q: What controversial internet practice does Algeria engage in during national exams?
options: Throttling internet speeds to prevent cheating
quiz.explanation: Algeria throttles internet speeds during national exams to prevent students from cheating, a practice that has been widely criticized as disproportionate to the concern.

laws.title: Torture and Ill-Treatment — Documented Practices
laws.subtitle: Algeria's legal prohibition and documented violations of torture
laws.fullDescription: Algeria ratified the UN Convention Against Torture in 1989. The constitution prohibits torture. However, international bodies including the UN Committee Against Torture and Human Rights Watch have documented ongoing torture and ill-treatment in detention, particularly in GID (intelligence service) facilities and during initial police detention. Methods documented include beatings, stress positions, and psychological pressure. The 2006 National Reconciliation Law effectively granted impunity to security forces for civil war-era torture. Individual prosecutions of security force members for torture are extremely rare. Algeria's human rights record was reviewed through the UN Universal Periodic Review mechanism.
laws.penalty: N/A — torture is formally prohibited; perpetrators rarely prosecuted in practice
exceptions: Military personnel subject to military justice system for abuse in custody
International monitoring bodies have very limited access to detention facilities
Diplomatic pressure has occasionally produced release of specific detainees

quiz.q: When did Algeria ratify the UN Convention Against Torture?
quiz.explanation: Algeria ratified the UN Convention Against Torture in 1989, though international bodies continue to document torture and ill-treatment in detention facilities, particularly in intelligence service custody.

laws.title: Port and Maritime Law — Algerian Shipping
laws.subtitle: Legal framework for Algeria's major Mediterranean ports
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's major ports — Algiers, Oran, Annaba, and Bejaia — handle the bulk of import/export trade. The National Port Authority manages port operations. Maritime law follows international UNCLOS conventions. Port congestion has historically been a major problem, with ships waiting weeks for berths — a significant cost to the economy. Port modernization programs using Chinese investment and management have improved some facilities. Cabotage (coastal shipping between Algerian ports) is reserved for Algerian vessels. The maritime sector also covers fishing rights in Algeria's Mediterranean Exclusive Economic Zone.
laws.penalty: Fines for maritime violations; vessel detention for safety failures; criminal prosecution for drug trafficking via ports
exceptions: Diplomatic vessels subject to international immunity conventions
Emergency vessel entry for distress situations cannot be refused
Fishing vessels under bilateral agreements have specific access rights

quiz.q: What has historically been a major problem at Algeria's ports?
options: Port congestion with ships waiting weeks for berths
quiz.explanation: Port congestion, with ships waiting weeks for berths, has historically been a major problem at Algeria's ports, creating significant economic costs for importers and exporters.

laws.title: Amazigh Spring Legacy and Cultural Rights
laws.subtitle: The 1980 Berber Cultural Movement and its legal legacy
laws.fullDescription: The Amazigh Spring (Printemps Berbère) of 1980, when Kabyle students and intellectuals rose up demanding Berber cultural and linguistic recognition, was a watershed moment. The movement was suppressed but planted seeds for later political pluralism. The Black Spring of 2001, when security forces killed 126 protesters in Kabylie, further radicalized the region. The movement's demands eventually led to Tamazight's national language status (2002), then official language status (2016). The MAK's 2021 designation as a terrorist organization has chilled cultural activism. The anniversary of the Amazigh Spring (April 20) remains a significant date for Kabyle identity.
laws.penalty: N/A — cultural rights context; MAK-linked activism subject to terrorism prosecution
exceptions: Cultural events commemorating the Amazigh Spring are permitted in principle
Academic study of Berber history and culture is protected
Traditional Amazigh cultural practices are not themselves criminalized

quiz.q: When did the Amazigh Spring (Printemps Berbère) take place?
quiz.explanation: The Amazigh Spring (Printemps Berbère) took place in 1980 when Kabyle students and intellectuals rose up demanding Berber cultural and linguistic recognition, laying groundwork for later pluralism.

laws.title: Drug Law and Kif (Cannabis) in Northern Algeria
laws.subtitle: Cannabis cultivation and trafficking laws
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has significant cannabis cultivation in the Rif Mountains-adjacent northern regions, though the major production is across the border in Morocco. Possession, trafficking, and cultivation of cannabis and other illegal drugs are criminalized under the 2004 Health Law. Cannabis (kif) use has traditional roots in some northern communities. Algeria is a transit route for Moroccan cannabis (hashish) destined for Europe. Drug trafficking organizations operating in the Sahel region increasingly intersect with Algerian criminal networks. Anti-narcotics units of the Algerian National Gendarmerie make significant seizures.
laws.penalty: 1–10 years imprisonment for possession; 10–20 years for trafficking; enhanced for organized networks
exceptions: Medical cannabis research has very limited authorization
Border community traditional use treated with some practical tolerance
Cooperation with anti-trafficking authorities can reduce sentences

quiz.q: What is Algeria's role in North African cannabis trafficking?
options: Primarily a transit route for Moroccan cannabis destined for Europe
quiz.explanation: Algeria is primarily a transit route for Moroccan cannabis (hashish) destined for Europe, with anti-narcotics units making significant seizures of trans-shipment drug trafficking.

laws.title: Traditional Medicine and Herbal Remedies Regulation
laws.subtitle: Legal framework for traditional healing practices
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has a rich tradition of herbal and traditional medicine, particularly in Berber and Saharan communities. The Ministry of Health regulates the sale of medicinal plants through licensed herbal pharmacies. Traditional healers ('thbibs') operate in a grey legal area — their practice is not formally licensed but is tolerated. The national pharmacopoeia includes recognized traditional remedies. During COVID-19, traditional remedies gained popularity amid vaccine hesitancy. The Hoggar region's Tuareg communities maintain distinct healing traditions. Counterfeit medicines sold in informal markets pose public health risks.
laws.penalty: Fines for unlicensed sale of controlled herbal medicines; criminal prosecution for harmful traditional treatments
exceptions: Traditional healers operating within community settings face minimal enforcement
Herbal pharmacies with licenses can sell traditional plant remedies
Research institutions may study traditional medicine under academic protocols

quiz.q: How is traditional medicine practice ('thbibs') regulated in Algeria?
options: Operates in a grey area — not formally licensed but tolerated
quiz.explanation: Traditional healers ('thbibs') in Algeria operate in a grey legal area — their practice is not formally licensed but is generally tolerated, particularly in rural and Berber communities.

laws.title: Sahara Desert Conservation and Biodiversity
laws.subtitle: Protection of Algeria's unique Saharan ecosystems
laws.fullDescription: The Algerian Sahara contains unique ecosystems including the Hoggar (Ahaggar) and Tassili n'Ajjer massifs — the latter a UNESCO World Heritage Site containing ancient rock art and rare flora. Protected area laws cover Ahaggar National Park (one of Africa's largest by area) and Tassili N'Ajjer National Park. The Saharan cheetah (among the world's rarest), Barbary macaque, and various endemic reptiles are protected species. Petroleum exploration in protected areas is a tension point. Sand extraction for construction from sensitive desert areas is regulated. Tourism development in the Sahara is promoted but faces security restrictions.
laws.penalty: Fines and imprisonment for poaching protected species; facility fines for unauthorized extraction
exceptions: Traditional Tuareg pastoralism recognized in national park buffer zones
Scientific expeditions with Ministry authorization permitted
Tourism operators licensed by Ministry of Tourism may access protected areas

quiz.q: What UNESCO World Heritage Site in Algeria contains ancient rock art?
quiz.explanation: Tassili n'Ajjer is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the Algerian Sahara containing ancient rock art and unique biodiversity, protected under Algeria's national park system.

laws.title: Cultural Policy and Arts Regulation
laws.subtitle: Algeria's support for and control of cultural expression
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has a rich cultural heritage — Berber, Arab, and French-influenced — reflected in its cinema (one of Africa's strongest), music (raï, chaabi, Kabyle), and visual arts. The Ministry of Culture funds cultural programs and venues. Raï music, born in Oran, gained global recognition but faced Islamist opposition in the 1990s — several raï artists were assassinated. Cinema is supported through the CADC (Algerian Centre for Cinematographic Development). Political content in arts faces the same speech restrictions as other media — films critical of government or military have faced censorship. Algeria's Constantine and Tlemcen served as Capitals of Arab Culture.
laws.penalty: Content restrictions apply to cultural works deemed harmful to national unity or insulting to Islam
exceptions: Historical films about the independence war ('moudjahid' tradition) receive strong state support
International co-productions may face less censorship pressure
Traditional folk music and dance forms are officially celebrated

quiz.q: What music genre born in Oran, Algeria faced violent opposition in the 1990s?
quiz.explanation: Raï music, born in Oran, gained global recognition but faced violent Islamist opposition in the 1990s during the civil war — several raï artists including Cheb Hasni were assassinated.

laws.title: Surveillance Law and Communications Interception
laws.subtitle: Algeria's legal framework for electronic surveillance
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's intelligence services have broad powers to intercept communications under the anti-terrorism framework and intelligence service statute. The Code of Criminal Procedure provides for judicial wiretapping authorization, but intelligence services operate under separate authorities with minimal oversight. Reports from activists and journalists suggest pervasive surveillance of political opponents, Hirak participants, and Kabyle activists. Algeria has acquired surveillance technology from European companies, as documented by the Privacy International organization. There is no meaningful independent oversight of intelligence surveillance operations.
laws.penalty: N/A — surveillance authorized under intelligence law; unauthorized private surveillance is criminal
exceptions: Judicial authorization required for law enforcement wiretapping in criminal cases
Attorney-client privilege nominally protects lawyer-client communications
Foreign diplomat communications have limited protection under Vienna Conventions

quiz.q: What organization has documented Algeria's acquisition of European surveillance technology?
quiz.explanation: Privacy International has documented Algeria's acquisition of surveillance technology from European companies, raising concerns about the technology's use against political opponents and activists.

laws.title: Decentralization — Wilaya System of Local Governance
laws.subtitle: Algeria's 58 provinces and local government structure
laws.fullDescription: Algeria is divided into 48 wilayas (provinces) — increased to 58 by presidential decree in 2019 to create new provinces in the Saharan south. Each wilaya is headed by a wali (governor) appointed by the president. Communal Popular Assemblies (APC) are elected local bodies. The centralized system gives central government dominant control — wilayas have limited fiscal and policy autonomy. Saharan wilayas were created partly to extend administrative presence and reduce the sense of southern neglect given the concentration of oil/gas infrastructure in the south with limited local benefit.
laws.penalty: N/A — administrative structure
exceptions: Greater Algiers has a metropolitan authority with additional powers
Wilaya councils can pass local development plans but require central approval
Emergency security powers can override normal local governance

laws.title: Renewable Energy Workforce Development
laws.subtitle: Algeria's plans for green economy job creation
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has committed to developing renewable energy to reduce domestic fossil fuel consumption (which consumes 30% of hydrocarbons production) and free up more for export. The 2015 Renewable Energy Program targeted 27% renewable electricity by 2030. Solar projects in the Sahara — Algeria has among the world's highest solar irradiation — are central to this strategy. The program aims to create over 100,000 jobs in the renewable sector. Partnerships with European and Chinese companies involve local content and training requirements. Despite the potential, progress has been slower than targets due to financing constraints and bureaucratic obstacles.

laws.title: Judicial Independence and Court System
laws.subtitle: Algeria's court structure and concerns about judicial independence
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's court system comprises communal courts (first instance), courts of appeal, and the Supreme Court. The Constitutional Council reviews legislation for constitutional compliance. Judges are formally independent but the executive has significant influence through the Superior Council of Magistracy (chaired by the president), appointments, and assignment decisions. Human rights organizations document judges following executive preferences in political cases. The State Security Court handles terrorism and national security cases. Corruption in the judiciary has been documented, with some judges prosecuted in post-Bouteflika crackdowns.
