laws.title: Language Policy — Arabic as the Official Language
laws.subtitle: Algeria's constitutional Arabization and its social impact
laws.fullDescription: Arabic is Algeria's primary official language under the constitution (alongside Tamazight since 2016). The Arabization policy pursued since independence replaced French in official functions, education, and government. In practice, Algerian Arabic (Darija), French, and Tamazight coexist in daily life. French remains dominant in business, higher education, and technical sectors. The constitutional designation of Arabic has created language tensions — Francophone Algerians (particularly educated elites) feel disadvantaged, while Arabists see French as a colonial legacy. This tension intersects with Islamist politics (Arabists tend to be more Islamist in orientation).

laws.title: Sovereign Wealth and Oil Stabilization Fund
laws.subtitle: Algeria's oil revenues fund and fiscal management
laws.fullDescription: Algeria established the Revenue Regulation Fund (FRR) in 2000 to manage oil revenue volatility. At its peak in 2013, the fund held over $77 billion. Falling oil prices from 2014 and continued government spending drained the fund — it was depleted to near zero by 2017. Algeria then resorted to unorthodox monetary financing (printing money) to cover deficits in 2017–2019, raising inflation concerns. The FRR's depletion reflected structural failure to diversify the economy during the boom years. Fiscal consolidation programs have been implemented but face social resistance. Algeria's fiscal breakeven oil price (the price needed to balance the budget) is among the highest in OPEC.

laws.title: Tsunami and Natural Disaster Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's disaster risk management and seismic risk
laws.fullDescription: Algeria is seismically active — the 2003 Boumerdès earthquake killed over 2,200 people and displaced 200,000. Building codes require seismic resistance standards in construction. The National Agency for Seismic Engineering (CGS) monitors seismic activity and enforces construction standards. Disaster response is coordinated through Civil Protection authorities. Algeria is also vulnerable to flash floods in northern mountainous regions. Climate change is increasing wildfire and drought risk. The Mediterranean coast faces tsunami risk from Algerian fault systems. Emergency preparedness planning has improved since 2003 but implementation remains uneven.

laws.title: National Liberation War Legacy — Legal and Political Status
laws.subtitle: The independence war's continuing influence on Algerian law and politics
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's 1954–1962 war of independence against France is the foundational legitimizing event for the entire political system. The FLN's role as the liberation movement grants it constitutional and cultural primacy. The National Organization of Moudjahideen (freedom fighters) has a constitutionally recognized status, and veterans and their families receive special benefits. The Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation extends this legitimizing framework to counter-terrorist operations. Criticism of the FLN's independence war conduct — including the wartime execution of rival nationalist MNA members — is socially and legally sensitive. November 1 (revolution day) is the most important national holiday.

quiz.q: What date does Algeria celebrate as its National Revolution Day?
quiz.explanation: November 1 is Algeria's most important national holiday — Revolution Day — marking the beginning of the independence war against France in 1954, the FLN's foundational legitimizing event.

laws.title: Contraband and Cross-Border Smuggling Law
laws.subtitle: Enforcement against smuggling across Algeria's vast desert borders
laws.fullDescription: Algeria shares vast desert borders with Morocco, Mali, Niger, Libya, Tunisia, and Mauritania — totaling over 6,000 km. Smuggling of fuel, consumer goods, cigarettes, weapons, drugs, and people across these porous borders is extensive. Algeria's Gendarmerie Nationale has specialized desert units for border enforcement. Fuel smuggling is particularly significant — Algeria's heavily subsidized domestic fuel prices make arbitrage enormously profitable. Weapons smuggling has been a security concern following the Libya conflict and Sahel instability. Border communities traditionally relied on informal trade for livelihoods.

laws.title: Food Security and Agricultural Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's agricultural policy and food import dependency
laws.fullDescription: Algeria imports approximately 45% of its food needs, creating significant food security vulnerability. The government subsidizes basic foodstuffs (semolina, bread, oil, sugar) through the Office National Interprofessionnel des Céréales (OAIC). Agricultural land is limited to northern Algeria — the south is desert. The Mitidja plain south of Algiers was historically Algeria's breadbasket. Agricultural policy promotes import substitution and privatization of some state farms. Greenhouse farming and drip irrigation programs have expanded production. The subsidized food system costs approximately $3 billion annually and is politically difficult to reform.

laws.title: Hirak Protest Prosecutions — Key Legal Charges
laws.subtitle: Laws used to prosecute Hirak movement participants
laws.fullDescription: The Algerian government has used multiple legal provisions to arrest and prosecute Hirak movement participants. Key charges include: Penal Code Article 79 (undermining state authority), Article 96 (harming national unity), Article 100 (attacking the morale of the army), anti-terrorism provisions, and flag laws (carrying Amazigh or Rif flags deemed 'foreign' flags). Over 200 activists were imprisoned simultaneously at the peak of crackdowns. Amnesty International recognized many as prisoners of conscience. Courts have sentenced activists to prison terms of 1–10 years. Internationally, the crackdowns were condemned by the EU, US State Department, and human rights organizations.

laws.title: Mining Law and Mineral Resources
laws.subtitle: Algeria's mining sector regulation beyond hydrocarbons
laws.fullDescription: Beyond hydrocarbons, Algeria has significant mineral resources including iron ore (Ghar Djebilet — one of the world's largest deposits), phosphate, zinc, and gold. The Mining Law of 2001, revised in 2014, governs exploration and extraction licences. State companies FERPHOS (phosphate) and FERAAL (iron) manage key mineral operations. The Ghar Djebilet iron ore project has attracted major Chinese investment (China Steel Express). Infrastructure — railway and water — remains a constraint on mining development in the remote Saharan south. Algeria aims to develop its mining sector as part of economic diversification.

laws.title: Press Freedom and Journalist Prosecutions

laws.fullDescription: Algeria consistently ranks among the lowest in press freedom indices — RSF ranked Algeria 145th out of 180 countries in 2023. The Penal Code, anti-terrorism law, and national reconciliation law are all used to prosecute journalists. The Algerian Journalists Syndicate (SAJ), created in 2012, has limited effectiveness. Both state and private media self-censor heavily. Foreign journalists face accreditation restrictions and surveillance. The 2021 arrest of journalist Khaled Drareni — who received a 3-year sentence for reporting on Hirak protests — became an international cause célèbre. Several journalists remain imprisoned as of 2024.

laws.title: Tourism Law and Sahara Tourism Development
laws.subtitle: Algeria's framework for developing its tourism sector
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has immense tourism potential — Sahara landscapes, Roman ruins (Djemila, Timgad — both UNESCO sites), Tassili cave art, and Mediterranean coastline — but is one of the least-visited North African countries due to visa restrictions, security concerns (Sahara travel advisories), and underdeveloped tourism infrastructure. The Ministry of Tourism manages licensing of operators. Visa requirements for most nationalities are restrictive. The 2015 opening of visa-free access for some Arab nationals was limited. Security restrictions on Sahara tourism following kidnapping incidents (including AQIM activity) have limited that sector. The government has identified tourism diversification as a development priority.

laws.title: Sub-Saharan Migration Transit — Legal and Humanitarian Issues

The main routes go through Niger/Mali to southern Algeria, then north to the Mediterranean coast. Algeria has conducted mass deportations — over 25,000 annually in some years — often abandoning migrants at desert border points without adequate provisions. Human Rights Watch and IOM have documented deaths from these conditions. Algeria has no asylum system — it is not party to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Migrants who complete the crossing often attempt to reach Spain via Morocco or Tunisia. Racism toward sub-Saharan migrants in Algeria is documented.

Its nine members serve 6-year terms, three appointed by the president, three by parliament, and three by the Supreme Court. The council has historically been deferential to executive preferences and has not served as an independent check on presidential power. It has been used to exclude opposition presidential candidates from elections.

laws.title: University Student Activism and Campus Law

laws.title: Mediterranean Coastal Zone Protection Law

The Coastal Zone Law prohibits construction within 100 meters of the sea in principle, though enforcement has been poor — illegal coastal construction is widespread. Coastal water pollution from urban sewage and industrial discharge is a documented problem. The Mediterranean Action Plan (MAP/UNEP) includes Algeria. Tourism development along the coast has been ambitious but poorly regulated. Climate change threatens to accelerate coastal erosion.

Teenage pregnancy rates are relatively low by regional standards. The state has not promoted family planning as aggressively as some neighbors (like Tunisia), and fertility rates remain higher. Youth (under 30) constitute over 60% of Algeria's population.

All associations must register with the Ministry of Interior, which has broad discretion to refuse or suspend registration. Foreign funding requires government authorization. Associations linked to the Hirak or human rights monitoring have been denied registration or suspended. International organizations must have approved agreements with the government. The law has been used to prevent formation of independent human rights monitoring groups. Bar association independence has also been contested.
laws.penalty: Criminal charges for operating unregistered associations; fines and dissolution for registered associations violating the law
exceptions: Professional associations (lawyers, doctors) operate under separate professional law
Religious associations registered through Ministry of Religious Affairs face different rules
Charitable associations with purely apolitical missions face lighter scrutiny

quiz.q: Which ministry in Algeria has discretion to refuse or suspend association registrations?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's Ministry of Interior has broad discretion to refuse or suspend association registrations under the 2012 Associations Law, giving it significant power to restrict civil society.

laws.title: Police Powers and Detention Without Charge
laws.subtitle: Algeria's police custody rules and documented abuses
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Code of Criminal Procedure allows police to hold suspects for up to 48 hours (garde à vue) without charge, renewable by a prosecutor's authorization for serious crimes. Anti-terrorism suspects can be held for up to 12 days in extended garde à vue. GID (intelligence) detention operates under separate, less transparent rules. Human rights organizations document that detainees are frequently held beyond legal limits, denied access to lawyers during the initial period, and subjected to ill-treatment. The right to notify family is provided by law but often violated in practice for political detainees.
laws.penalty: N/A — police custody framework; officers conducting illegal detentions theoretically liable but rarely prosecuted
exceptions: Juvenile detainees must be held in separate facilities with shorter detention limits
Medical emergencies must result in access to healthcare during custody
Diplomatic detainees subject to international notification requirements

quiz.q: How long can Algerian police hold terrorism suspects in extended custody without charge?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's anti-terrorism provisions allow police to hold terrorism suspects for up to 12 days in extended garde à vue — six times the standard 48-hour limit, with documented cases of exceeding even this extended period.

laws.title: Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances
laws.subtitle: Algeria's formal and practical distribution of governmental power
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's constitution provides for separation of executive, legislative, and judicial powers. In practice, the executive (dominated by the president and military) has overwhelming dominance. Parliament (bicameral — National People's Assembly and Council of the Nation) has limited independent legislative initiative and rarely challenges executive proposals. The Constitutional Council (now Court) has been deferential. The judiciary lacks independence. Anti-corruption prosecutions since 2019 have been selectively used as a political tool rather than systematic accountability. Algeria's power structure is often described by analysts as a 'deep state' of military, intelligence, and civilian elite with formal democratic institutions as a facade.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional structure
exceptions: Constitutional amendments require parliamentary supermajority or referendum
Budget law requires parliamentary approval — a nominal check
International treaty ratification requires parliamentary consent

quiz.q: How is Algeria's power structure commonly described by political analysts?
options: 'Deep state' of military and elite with formal institutions as a facade
quiz.explanation: Algeria's power structure is commonly described by analysts as a 'deep state' of military, intelligence, and civilian elite, with formal democratic institutions (parliament, courts) functioning as a largely decorative facade.

laws.title: Cultural Heritage Protection Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's framework for protecting archaeological sites
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has extraordinary archaeological heritage — Carthaginian, Roman, Byzantine, Arab, Ottoman, and indigenous Berber sites. UNESCO World Heritage Sites include Djemila, Tipasa, Timgad, the Qal'a of the Beni Hammad, Tassili n'Ajjer, and the Casbah of Algiers. The Heritage Protection Law prohibits unauthorized excavation and export of antiquities. Trafficking of antiquities — Algeria has significant looting problems in less-policed interior sites — is criminalized. The National Center of Prehistoric, Anthropological and Historical Research (CNRPAH) oversees heritage. Some heritage sites have suffered from neglect and inappropriate development in their buffer zones.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment and fines for illegal excavation and antiquity trafficking; asset confiscation
exceptions: Authorized archaeological missions with government permission can conduct excavations
Registered private collections of antiquities may be grandfathered
International cooperation for study of cultural property has some exemptions

quiz.q: How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites does Algeria have?
quiz.explanation: Algeria has six or more UNESCO World Heritage Sites including Djemila, Tipasa, Timgad, the Qal'a of the Beni Hammad, Tassili n'Ajjer, and the Casbah of Algiers — reflecting its extraordinary archaeological heritage.

laws.title: Internet Access Rights and Digital Governance
laws.subtitle: Algeria's emerging digital rights framework
laws.fullDescription: Algeria does not have a constitutional right to internet access. The state controls key telecommunications infrastructure through Algérie Télécom. Internet shutdowns or slowdowns have been used during politically sensitive periods. The ARPT regulates the telecom sector but lacks independence from government direction. Algeria's internet infrastructure is concentrated in the north — significant digital divides exist between urban and rural areas and between north and south. The 2018 data protection law addresses some digital rights but surveillance provisions undermine privacy. Algeria has not joined international open internet frameworks.
laws.penalty: N/A — no explicit right being violated since no legal right exists; unauthorized blocking by private actors could be illegal
exceptions: Academic and research networks may have different access agreements
VPN usage is common and technically illegal but enforcement is inconsistent
Emergency communications must remain operational even during partial shutdowns

quiz.q: What digital divide is significant within Algeria?
options: North-south divide between urban and rural areas
Language-based divide between Arabic and French internet
quiz.explanation: A significant digital divide exists within Algeria between the urban, industrialized north and the rural and Saharan south, with internet infrastructure heavily concentrated in northern cities.

laws.title: Sahel Security Operations and Counter-Terrorism
laws.subtitle: Algeria's military operations against AQIM and Sahel terrorist groups
laws.fullDescription: Algeria has been at the forefront of counter-terrorism in the Sahel region since the GIA conflicts of the 1990s. AQIM (Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb), formed from the Algerian GSPC, continues to operate in the Sahara-Sahel zone. Algeria rejected foreign military intervention in Mali (2012) and the Sahel but provides intelligence and border security cooperation. The In Amenas gas facility hostage crisis (January 2013) demonstrated continued terrorist threat — 39 foreign workers were killed. Algeria's Tamanrasset conference coordinates Sahel security with Mali, Niger, and Mauritania. Drone operations and special forces are deployed in the deep Sahara.
laws.penalty: Death penalty and life imprisonment for terrorism causing deaths; heavy sentences for material support
exceptions: Amnesty provisions for surrendering militants under 2006 framework continue to be available
Border community members may receive lighter treatment for indirect support
Intelligence cooperation with foreign services sometimes involves procedural shortcuts

quiz.q: How many foreign workers were killed in the January 2013 In Amenas hostage crisis?
quiz.explanation: The January 2013 In Amenas gas facility hostage crisis, carried out by an AQIM-linked group, resulted in the deaths of 39 foreign workers from multiple countries.

laws.title: Music and Entertainment Regulation
laws.subtitle: Algeria's approach to popular culture and entertainment venues
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's entertainment sector operates under mixed regulations — concert venues require licences, foreign artists need visa approvals and content reviews, and music festivals require authorization. Raï music remains Algeria's most globally recognized musical export. Kabyle music (Imazighen tradition) has deep cultural roots. The annual Timgad International Festival (held at the Roman ruins of Timgad since 1969) is a major cultural event. Religious conservatives and Islamist influence has periodically restricted concerts and mixed-gender entertainment. The government has invested in cultural centres but also used cultural events politically.
laws.penalty: Fines for unlicensed entertainment venues; cancellation of events without authorization; content-based prosecution for material deemed immoral
exceptions: Traditional music and cultural events in rural areas face less formal licensing requirements
State-organized cultural events bypass standard authorization procedures
International co-productions with cultural ministry support face fewer restrictions

quiz.q: Where is Algeria's famous Timgad International Festival held?
options: At the Roman ruins of Timgad
quiz.explanation: The Timgad International Festival, held since 1969, takes place at the Roman ruins of Timgad in northeastern Algeria, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that serves as an atmospheric cultural venue.

laws.title: Energy Transition and Domestic Gas Subsidy Reform
laws.subtitle: Algeria's challenge of reducing costly domestic energy subsidies
laws.fullDescription: Algeria heavily subsidizes domestic energy prices — Algerians pay among the world's lowest prices for petrol, gas, and electricity. Total energy subsidies cost approximately $10–15 billion annually. Reforming these subsidies is politically explosive — 1988 bread price riots that preceded democratization and Hirak were partly driven by subsidy cut fears. The IMF and World Bank have urged subsidy reform as part of fiscal consolidation. Some incremental increases have been implemented but far short of market prices. Energy subsidy reform requires simultaneously developing a social protection system to cushion the impact on the poor.
laws.penalty: N/A — energy pricing policy
exceptions: Industrial users pay different (higher) rates than residential customers
Agricultural fuel subsidies partially separate from consumer energy subsidies
Export-oriented industries may have different energy pricing frameworks

quiz.q: Approximately how much do Algeria's energy subsidies cost annually?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's energy subsidies, which give Algerians among the world's lowest fuel and electricity prices, cost approximately $10–15 billion annually — a major fiscal burden that is politically difficult to reform.

laws.title: Prison System and Detention Conditions
laws.subtitle: Algeria's penitentiary system and conditions in custody
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's prison system holds tens of thousands of inmates, including a significant and growing number of political prisoners since the Hirak crackdowns. El Harrach prison in Algiers is one of Africa's largest and most overcrowded. Conditions have been documented as poor — overcrowding, inadequate healthcare, and ill-treatment. The National Commission for the Promotion and Protection of Human Rights (CNCPPDH) theoretically oversees conditions but lacks independence. Independent monitoring organizations have limited access. The 2019–2022 wave of political arrests significantly increased the prison population of activists and journalists.
laws.penalty: N/A — detention framework; prison staff misconduct subject to disciplinary action
exceptions: Women held in separate facilities with different standards
Political prisoners may have access to lawyers, though this is often restricted in practice
Foreign prisoners subject to consular notification requirements

quiz.q: What is El Harrach prison in Algiers notable for?
options: Being one of Africa's largest and most overcrowded prisons
quiz.explanation: El Harrach prison in Algiers is one of Africa's largest and most overcrowded prisons, with documented poor conditions including inadequate healthcare and reports of ill-treatment.

laws.title: Small Business and Entrepreneurship Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's framework for SME development and formalization
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's informal economy dominates small business — many small traders and entrepreneurs operate outside the formal system to avoid taxes and regulatory requirements. The National Agency for the Support and Development of Entrepreneurship (ANADE) provides support for formal small businesses. Youth employment programs linked to the National Unemployment Insurance Fund (CNAC) enable small business creation. Administrative barriers to business formalization are significant — the World Bank's Doing Business reports ranked Algeria poorly for business regulations. The government has made efforts to simplify procedures through one-stop-shop investment centers.
laws.penalty: Fines for tax evasion and informal trading in regulated sectors; social security contribution penalties
exceptions: Street vendors in designated areas tolerated under certain conditions
Agricultural small businesses have simplified registration
Start-up visa programs for tech entrepreneurs have streamlined procedures

quiz.q: What organization provides support for formal small businesses in Algeria?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's ANADE (National Agency for the Support and Development of Entrepreneurship) provides support for formal small businesses, including youth employment programs linked to the National Unemployment Insurance Fund.

laws.title: Presidential Election — 2024 and Tebboune Re-election
laws.subtitle: Algeria's 2024 presidential election and democratic legitimacy questions
laws.fullDescription: President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, who came to power in the controversial December 2019 election amid Hirak boycotts, won re-election in September 2024 with an officially reported 94.7% of the vote in a first-round victory. Voter turnout was officially reported at 48% but independent observers and opposition parties disputed both figures. The main opposition candidates were either excluded by the Constitutional Court or lacked genuine competitiveness. International observers noted concerns about the lack of level playing field. The election result was condemned by Hirak-aligned groups as a continuation of military-backed rule without democratic legitimacy.
laws.penalty: N/A — electoral result; electoral fraud allegations are not formally investigated
exceptions: Opposition candidates who competed accepted the process
International diplomatic recognition of results followed quickly
Some domestic journalists who reported on irregularities face prosecution

quiz.q: What was Tebboune's officially reported vote share in Algeria's September 2024 presidential election?
quiz.explanation: President Tebboune was officially reported to have won 94.7% of the vote in Algeria's September 2024 presidential election, a result questioned by opposition groups and independent observers.

laws.title: National Parks and Nature Reserve System
laws.subtitle: Algeria's protected natural areas beyond the Sahara
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's Mediterranean and Tell Atlas regions contain significant biodiversity — the Numidia National Park, El Kala National Park (a major wetland and Ramsar site), and Chrea National Park are key protected areas. The Barbary macaque (Macaca sylvanus) — North Africa's only wild primate — is found in Atlas Mountain forests. Atlas cedars in the Cedrus atlantica forests are an iconic species. Hunting regulations protect endangered species. Deforestation, overgrazing, and wildfires threaten these ecosystems. The ONFS (National Office for Forests) manages forest conservation.
laws.penalty: Fines and imprisonment for poaching and unauthorized hunting; habitat destruction charges for developers
exceptions: Traditional rural communities with historical use rights in buffer zones
Scientific research with authorized permits
Managed hunting of non-protected species with licences

quiz.q: What is North Africa's only wild primate species, found in Algeria's Atlas Mountains?
quiz.explanation: The Barbary macaque (Macaca sylvanus) is North Africa's only wild primate species, found in Algeria's Atlas Mountain forests and protected under Algeria's nature reserve system.

laws.title: Flag and National Symbol Protection Law
laws.subtitle: Criminal penalties for desecrating Algerian national symbols
laws.fullDescription: Algeria criminalizes desecration of the national flag and other national symbols. The Penal Code provides penalties for attacks on national symbols. During the Hirak, authorities controversially prosecuted protesters for carrying the Amazigh (Berber) flag — arguing that displaying a non-national flag at protests was illegal. The same provision was used against those carrying Palestinian flags in some contexts. The Algerian flag (green and white with red crescent and star) is a powerful national symbol linked to the independence struggle. Military and state symbols also have legal protection from desecration.
laws.penalty: 6 months–2 years imprisonment and fines for desecrating national flag or symbols
exceptions: Foreign flags may be flown at diplomatic premises and official international events
Historical display of flags in museums and educational contexts protected
National sports teams' use of flags in international competition not restricted

quiz.q: What unusual flag-related prosecution occurred during Algeria's Hirak protests?
options: Protesters were charged for defacing the national flag
Protesters were charged for carrying the Amazigh (Berber) flag deemed an illegal foreign flag
Protesters were charged for flying French flags
Protesters were charged for using unofficial flag variants
quiz.explanation: Algerian authorities controversially prosecuted Hirak protesters for carrying the Amazigh (Berber) flag, characterizing it as displaying an illegal foreign flag — a charge widely condemned by human rights organizations.

laws.title: Construction and Real Estate Market Regulation
laws.subtitle: Algeria's housing market dynamics and regulatory challenges
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's real estate market is distorted by massive state intervention in housing construction (AADL, OPGI programs) alongside a private sector that operates in both formal and informal markets. Land prices in Algiers are among North Africa's highest despite controls. The Algerian Construction Professional Registry (CNBTP) regulates contractors. Informal construction — building without permits or beyond permit specifications — is widespread. Price controls on public housing are strictly maintained but create black markets for unit allocation. Property transaction taxes and registration fees are significant. Foreign ownership of real estate faces restrictions similar to investment restrictions.
laws.penalty: Fines and demolition for unauthorized construction; criminal prosecution for fraudulent property transactions
exceptions: Social housing tenants have preferential purchase rights at fixed prices
Agricultural land conversion requires special authorization
Heritage zone properties subject to additional restrictions and support mechanisms

quiz.q: What characterizes Algiers real estate prices by North African standards?
options: Among the cheapest in North Africa
Among the highest in North Africa despite state controls
quiz.explanation: Land and property prices in Algiers are among the highest in North Africa despite government price controls, driven by housing demand and distortions from the massive public housing program.

laws.title: COVID-19 Health Messaging and Vaccine Hesitancy Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's pandemic communication challenges and public health authority
laws.fullDescription: Algeria faced significant COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy — surveys showed among the highest hesitancy rates in Africa. This was driven by Islamic religious concerns about vaccine ingredients, distrust of state institutions following the Hirak, and social media misinformation. The government used the Defence Law (rather than specific health legislation) to enforce health measures. Social media misinformation about COVID was prosecuted under existing speech laws. Algeria received vaccines through COVAX and bilateral agreements with China (Sinovac), Russia (Sputnik), and Western manufacturers. Vaccine mandate proposals were abandoned given political sensitivity.
laws.penalty: Fines for violating pandemic health orders; prosecution for spreading medical misinformation
exceptions: Medical contraindications recognized as exemption from vaccination where implemented
Religious exemption claims were not formally recognized
Healthcare workers faced stronger pressure to vaccinate though no formal mandate was enacted

quiz.q: Which law did Algeria primarily use to enforce COVID-19 health measures?
quiz.explanation: Algeria used the Defence Law (rather than specific health legislation) to enforce COVID-19 measures, enabling executive action without parliamentary approval during the pandemic.

laws.title: National Statistics and Economic Data Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's official statistics framework and data transparency
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's National Office of Statistics (ONS) collects and publishes economic and social data. Data transparency has been a concern — unemployment statistics, poverty rates, and informal economy estimates from official sources are often disputed by independent economists and international organizations. The ONS operates under the authority of the Prime Minister's office. Budget data publication has improved under fiscal reform pressure. Algeria does not publish detailed breakdown of military spending. The lack of independent statistical verification has been used to question the credibility of election results (including turnout figures) and economic performance data.
laws.penalty: N/A — statistical agency; misinformation about economic data in context of securities or financial fraud subject to criminal law
exceptions: Academic institutions may conduct independent surveys with government authorization
International organizations like IMF and World Bank publish independent assessments
Some regional data collection done through wilaya statistical offices

quiz.q: Under whose authority does Algeria's National Office of Statistics (ONS) operate?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's National Office of Statistics (ONS) operates under the authority of the Prime Minister's office, contributing to concerns about the independence of official statistical data.

laws.title: Hate Speech and Sectarian Incitement Law
laws.subtitle: Algeria's provisions against inciting religious or ethnic division
laws.fullDescription: Algeria criminalizes speech inciting religious or ethnic discord under Penal Code Article 96 (national unity) and related provisions. The application of these laws has been highly asymmetric — while they theoretically protect all groups, in practice they have been used most often against Kabyle Berber activists, Ahmadi Muslims (considered heretical), and critics of the FLN rather than against anti-Berber or anti-minority speech. Saharan Tuareg and Mozabite Ibadi Muslim communities face unofficial discrimination but have rarely seen their persecutors prosecuted under hate speech laws. The laws' selective application reflects the broader pattern of political instrumentalization of the legal system.
laws.penalty: 6 months–3 years imprisonment for inciting religious or ethnic discord; enhanced penalties if resulting in violence
exceptions: Government-endorsed narratives promoting national unity are protected expression
Criticism of religious minorities framed as protecting Islam may receive different treatment
Academic and sociological analysis of inter-community tensions may be exempted

quiz.q: Against which groups have Algeria's hate speech and national unity laws most often been applied?
options: Against Kabyle Berber activists and Ahmadi Muslims
Against separatist movements in the south
quiz.explanation: Despite theoretically protecting all groups, Algeria's hate speech and national unity laws have most often been applied against Kabyle Berber activists, Ahmadi Muslims, and FLN critics — reflecting the political instrumentalization of these provisions.

laws.title: Sports Law and Football Governance
laws.subtitle: Algeria's sporting regulatory framework and football culture
laws.fullDescription: Football is Algeria's national passion — the national team's 2019 Africa Cup of Nations victory triggered massive celebrations nationwide, with Hirak protesters briefly adopting football scarves as symbols. Club football is governed by the Professional Football League (LFP). Match-fixing scandals and governance problems have plagued Algerian club football. The Ministry of Youth and Sports oversees sports associations. Algerian footballers in European leagues (particularly Riyad Mahrez and others) are national heroes. Stadium violence between supporters of rival clubs (notably Club Sportif Constantinois and Entente Sportive Sétif) has prompted legal responses.
laws.penalty: Fines and match bans for clubs involved in violence; criminal prosecution for stadium violence participants
exceptions: Youth development academies have separate registration from professional clubs
Traditional Kabyle games and Saharan sports have separate cultural heritage status
International competition appearances governed by FIFA regulations rather than domestic law
laws.sourceLabel: Algerian Ministry of Youth and Sports

quiz.q: What significant football achievement did Algeria celebrate in 2019?
options: First Algerian player in European Champions League
quiz.explanation: Algeria's national team's 2019 Africa Cup of Nations victory triggered massive nationwide celebrations, with protesters briefly adopting football imagery as symbols during the Hirak movement.

laws.title: Emergency Decree Powers and Royal Prerogative Equivalent
laws.subtitle: Algeria's presidential ordinance powers and legislative bypass
laws.fullDescription: Algeria's constitution grants the president power to issue ordinances (décrets exécutifs) with the force of law when parliament is not in session or in emergency circumstances. In practice, ordinances have been used to implement significant policy changes without full parliamentary debate. During parliament's recess periods, the executive has issued numerous ordinances covering economic policy, security measures, and social regulations. This presidential legislative power, combined with the military's influence, creates a system where formal parliamentary legislation is less significant than presidential and executive action. The Constitutional Court can review ordinances but rarely does so in ways that challenge executive preferences.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional executive power; violations of rights through ordinances addressable through Constitutional Court in theory
exceptions: Ordinances must be submitted to parliament when it next convenes for ratification
Permanent constitutional provisions cannot be modified by ordinance alone
International treaty obligations cannot be overridden by domestic ordinance

quiz.q: What presidential power allows Algeria's executive to bypass parliament with legally binding regulations?
quiz.explanation: Algeria's constitution grants the president power to issue ordinances (décrets exécutifs) with the force of law when parliament is not in session, enabling the executive to bypass parliamentary debate on significant policy changes.
